lessons.title: Rights and duties of the child and the citizen
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Social Studies (geography, history, citizenship); to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name important rights of children and the duties that go with them.
Explain that every right brings a responsibility.
Give examples of good behaviour at school and at home.
reviewNotes: Facts about Cameroon are limited to well-established, neutral points; dates and names to be checked by a teacher against the official textbook.
Child rights are listed in simplified form from the UN Convention; check that they match the wording of the official civic education syllabus. Mention of taxes applies to adults only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Rights and duties
blocks.md: A **right** is something that every person should have or may do. A **duty** is something we must do. Rights and duties go together: if I have a right, I must respect the same right of others. Children's rights are protected by the **Convention on the Rights of the Child** of the United Nations.

blocks.caption: Rights and duties go together.
blocks.alt: Two boxes side by side. The first says Rights: what you may have. The second says Duties: what you must do.

blocks.title: Rights of the child
blocks.md: Children have the right to: **life** and a **name**; **education**; **health care**; **food, clean water and a home**; **protection** from harm and from work that damages their health or school; **rest and play**; to be **heard** and to **practise their religion**; and to be treated **equally** whatever their sex, tribe or religion.

blocks.title: Duties of a pupil and a citizen
blocks.md: A pupil must: **respect** teachers, parents and other pupils; **obey** school rules; come **on time**; do homework; **look after** school property and keep the school clean. A citizen must: **obey the laws**, **respect** others and their property, **pay taxes** (adults), protect public property, and help to keep the community safe and clean.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking that rights mean we can do anything we like: my rights end where the rights of others begin.
- Thinking that only adults have rights.
- Forgetting that children also have duties.
- Breaking public property (a desk, a tap, a road sign): it belongs to everybody.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Right or duty? (a) Going to school. (b) Obeying the school rules.
steps: (a) Every child has the right to education.
(b) Obeying the rules is a duty of every pupil.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A pupil writes on the desk with a pen. Which duty is broken, and what should he do?
steps: The duty to look after school property.
He should say sorry, clean the desk and not do it again.
blocks.answer: He broke the duty to look after school property; he should say sorry and clean the desk.

objectives: Describe the flag, the motto and the anthem of Cameroon.
Name the three branches of government in a simple way.
Say who leads local communities and what a mayor does.
reviewNotes: Facts about Cameroon are limited to well-established, neutral points; dates and names to be checked by a teacher against the official textbook.

Colour meanings and the coat of arms description follow common school textbooks; check wording. Institutions (Senate, National Assembly, councils, courts) described in the simplest way. Anthem line is the English version's first words.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: National symbols
blocks.md: The **flag** has three vertical stripes, **green, red and yellow**, with a **yellow star** in the middle of the red stripe. The **motto** is **Peace – Work – Fatherland**. The **anthem** in English begins *O Cameroon, Cradle of Our Forefathers*. The **coat of arms** shows a shield with scales of justice and the motto. We show **respect** for the symbols: we stand when the anthem is played and when the flag is raised.

items.text: Flag of Cameroon: three vertical stripes and a star

blocks.caption: The flag of Cameroon.
blocks.alt: A flag with three vertical stripes, green on the left, red in the middle and yellow on the right. A yellow star is in the centre of the red stripe.

blocks.title: Meaning of the colours
blocks.md: Textbooks usually say: **green** stands for the forests and hope, **red** for unity, and **yellow** for the sun and the savanna of the north. The **star** stands for unity. The country uses the FCFA as its currency. Yaoundé is the capital.

blocks.title: How the country is governed
blocks.md: Government has three parts. The **executive** (the **President** and the ministers) runs the country. The **legislature** (the **National Assembly** and the **Senate**) makes the laws. The **judiciary** (the **courts** and judges) applies the laws. Locally, towns and villages have **councils** led by a **mayor** or a **chief** (fon, lamido) who looks after the community and its roads, markets and public places.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Putting the stripes in the wrong order or forgetting the star.
- Mixing the three branches: the courts do not make laws and the National Assembly does not judge cases.
- Showing disrespect to the flag or anthem as a joke.
- Thinking that the mayor and the President do the same job.

blocks.title: Example 1
steps: It has three vertical stripes: green, red, yellow (left to right).
A yellow star is in the middle of the red stripe.
blocks.answer: Three vertical stripes (green, red, yellow) with a yellow star on the red stripe.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Who makes laws and who applies them to settle cases?
steps: The National Assembly (and the Senate) makes laws.
The courts and judges apply them.
blocks.answer: Parliament makes the laws; the courts apply them.

lessons.title: Road safety and living together in the community
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Social Studies (geography, history, citizenship); to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Follow the rules for crossing the road and for being a passenger.
Know the meaning of the traffic lights and common road signs.
Describe how people live and work together in a community.
reviewNotes: Facts about Cameroon are limited to well-established, neutral points; dates and names to be checked by a teacher against the official textbook.

Road safety rules are general; local rules (helmet law, signs) should be checked by a teacher or the road safety authority. 'Look left, right and left again' is used because Cameroon drives on the right; some books say 'right then left'.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Crossing the road safely
blocks.md:
1. Stop at the **edge of the pavement**, not on the road.
2. Look **left, right and left again**; listen for vehicles.
3. Cross at a **zebra crossing** or a footbridge if there is one.
4. Walk straight across, do **not run**, and do not use your phone.
5. Never play football or other games on the road. Walk on the pavement or, if there is none, on the side facing the traffic.

blocks.caption: The traffic light.
blocks.alt: A grey traffic light with three lights. The red light means stop, the amber light means get ready, and the green light means go when it is safe.

blocks.title: Signs and passengers
blocks.md: **Triangle** signs warn (a school ahead, a bend). **Round** signs give an order or forbid something (stop, no entry). **Square or rectangular** signs give information (a hospital, a parking place). **Passengers**: fasten the seat belt, do not put your head or arm out of the window, and do not get in an overloaded vehicle. **Motorbike riders** must wear a helmet.

blocks.title: The community
blocks.md: A **community** is a group of people who live in the same place and help one another: a family, a school, a village or a town. People do different jobs: farmers, traders, teachers, nurses, drivers, builders, police. We keep our community clean, safe and peaceful by obeying rules, respecting chiefs and elders, helping neighbours, and sharing communal work.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Running across the road after a ball.
- Crossing between parked vehicles where drivers cannot see you.
- Thinking that a green light means 'go' even if a car is still coming: look first.
- Riding a motorbike without a helmet 'because the trip is short'.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: You want to cross a road at a zebra crossing. Say what you do, in order.
steps: Stop at the edge of the pavement, look left, right and left again.
When the road is clear, walk straight across without running.
blocks.answer: Stop, look left-right-left, then walk across without running.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why must a motorbike rider wear a helmet?
steps: In an accident the head can be badly hurt.
A helmet protects the head and can save a life.
blocks.answer: A helmet protects the head and can save a life.
